title: Farm plants may help fight infections, teen finds
content: *a_teen_girl_smiles_in_front_of_a_project_poster_titled_'field_of_dreams'_on_a_background_of_flowerin
Locklyn Ward, 14, investigated whether two dozen plants found on her family’s farm could help fight bacterial infections.

Locklyn Ward, 14, lives on a farm in Oklahoma. One evening while she was helping feed the cows, she got curious about the plants growing in the field. She knew that scientists are always searching for new ways to fight infections. So she set out to see if any of the plants growing on her family’s farm could take down bacteria.

Locklyn picked 24 plants; 12 were native to her state. She cut the plants into one-gram (four hundredths of an ounce) pieces and boiled each to extract chemicals from it. Then, she tested those extracts against two types of bacteria: Escherichia coli and Staphylococcus epidermidis. Locklyn also tested antibiotics that are currently used to treat infections.
*a_teen_girl_smiles_standing_in_front_of_a_pool_on_a_sunny_day
fCAs a member of the Cherokee Nation, Locklyn has always been interested in local plants’ traditional and medicinal uses.

The test involved paper disks soaked in either the plant extracts or current antibiotics. Locklyn placed those soaked disks into dishes containing bacteria. If chemicals from the farm plants had antibiotic powers, the bacteria around those paper disks would die.

No farm-plant extract worked as well as current medicines. But 13 of the 24 plants did kill some bacteria. These included seven native plants. Locklyn hopes her results may point to new ways to fight germs. Overuse of current antibiotics is leading to more drug-resistant bacteria, so new solutions are much needed.

Locklyn did this project as an eighth grader at Grove Middle School in Grove, Okla. Her research earned her a finalist spot in the 2026 Thermo Fisher Scientific Junior Innovators Challenge. This program is run by Society for Science, which also publishes Science News Explores. Here, Locklyn shares science-fair experiences and advice.

“Growing up, my grandmother often talked with me about how plants and herbs can be used for medicine and healing,” Locklyn says. “And as a citizen of the Cherokee Nation, I’ve always been interested in learning more about plants and their traditional and potential medicinal uses.”

“Managing my time, because I’m involved in many extracurriculars,” Locklyn says. With church activities and sports, her schedule is a bit chaotic, she says. Doing research required finding pockets of time on weekends and after school — and sometimes saying no to other fun plans. “I used Google Calendar,” she says. “That helped a lot.”

Locklyn’s science-fair teacher was a huge help. “She’s the one if I got bad results, she’d be like, ‘It’s okay, Locklyn, just keep going. You’re gonna get it.’” She was “very inspirational to me,” the teen says. “She’s the best.” Locklyn’s biggest piece of advice for science fair newbies is to find a mentor like this to help stay motivated through times of struggle and stress.

title: Scientists Say: Sanguivore
content: *a_vampire_bat_runs_across_dark_ground
Vampire bats, such as Desmodus rotundus, evolved limbs that allow them to run and jump with great agility. When seeking a blood meal, these bats may sprint after prey or creep up on sleeping animals.

iFhttps://w.soundcloud.com/player/?url=https%3A//api.soundcloud.com/tracks/soundcloud%253Atracks%253A2426110491&color=%23ff5500&auto_play=false&hide_related=false&show_comments=true&show_user=true&show_reposts=false&show_teaser=true
A sanguivore is an animal that eats blood.
Some species survive on blood alone. They are called obligate sanguivores. Bedbugs, ticks and vampire bats are examples.
Other species drink blood to supplement their diet. Or they drink blood only at certain stages of their life. Part-time blood drinkers are called facultative sanguivores.
Consider mosquitoes. They usually eat plant nectar. But female mosquitoes need the protein in blood to help them mature their eggs.

Oxpeckers are another example of part-time vampires. These birds perch atop grazing rhinos and zebras in the African savannah and pluck ticks from the animals’ hides. They also lap up blood at the wound site where the tick was. Sometimes these birds pick open old wounds on the animal’s hide for an extra blood snack.

Blood doesn’t have many nutrients and packs few calories. It consists mostly of water. Most foods contain easy-to-digest sugars and fats. But blood doesn’t contain much of either. Instead, most of blood’s calories come from proteins, which are harder to digest. Blood also comes loaded with iron. Animals need some iron in their diet. But the high levels found in blood can be toxic.

Animals that eat blood must handle these dietary challenges. Take vampire bats. The three species of them are the only known mammals that are obligate sanguivores. Specialized kidneys let vampire bats purge water quickly. In fact, they usually begin peeing while they eat. Their digestive systems absorb very little iron from their food. And their guts also host microbes that help them break down blood proteins. These microbes also create vitamins that the bats cannot get from blood.
The poor nutritional quality of blood probably explains why humans never evolved to drink it.

title: Your skin’s chemistry may affect which mosquitoes you attract
content: *a_mosquito-bitten_hand
Not all mosquitoes like the same people. Your skin’s chemistry and microbiome may influence how tasty different species find you.

Each summer, some people seem to get eaten alive by mosquitoes. Others sail through the season with nary a bite. Who those bloodsuckers prefer could trace to our body chemistry and which microbes live on our skin, a new study finds. And their taste preferences seem to vary by species.

Knowing how mosquitoes pick their human snacks could help prevent disease. With each bite, mosquitoes can spread illnesses that they may have picked up from an earlier blood meal, such as dengue and Zika.

“We want to understand what people’s risks are for being bitten,” says Matthew DeGennaro. He thinks the answer might be in the molecules — and the bacteria — found on our skin. DeGennaro works at Florida International University in Miami. There he studies how genetics influences the nervous system.
Scientists might use information from the new study to one day make someone’s smell less attractive to mosquitoes. Indeed, this could lead to new types of mosquito repellents, says DeGennaro.

Mosquitoes find meals using visual and scent cues (as well as their victims’ heat signatures). More than a thousand chemicals can go into making an individual’s scent. So it’s hard to know which most affect mosquitoes’ preferences as they search for their next blood meal. To figure this out, DeGennaro and his co-workers recruited 119 human targets.
Three species of mosquitoes sampled each volunteer’s unique scent. Scientists used a device that let caged mosquitoes smell these people but not bite them.
*a_person_puts_their_arm_into_a_clear_tube_full_of_mosquitoes

fCHuman volunteers put their arms into a device that allowed three species of mosquitoes to smell — but not bite — them. Researchers then measured how many mosquitoes came sniffing. The more attractive a species found each volunteer, the bigger the swarm that checked them out.

Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus mosquitoes feed by day. So volunteers could come to the lab during the day, place their arm inside the device and get sniffed. That wouldn’t work for Culex quinquefasciatus. Those bloodsuckers come out to feed only at night. To collect the volunteers’ scent for this species, each recruit had to wear a nylon sleeve for several hours. Then, at night, the researchers placed that sleeve into the device.

Scientists counted how many mosquitoes of each species entered the device to check out each person’s scent. That let them gauge how attracted they were to each human’s smell. They shared their findings August 21 in the journal iScience.
Each species preferred a different mix of volunteers. Some people were attractive to more than one species of mosquito. But no one person was the favorite of all three species.

Scientists have wondered why we might smell tasty to one mosquito species but not another. So the Florida group sampled chemical vapors in the air around each person’s arm. Then, they looked for which ones were found on the volunteers who were most attractive — or least attractive — to each species.

Ae. aegypti and C. quinquefasciatus were more attracted to people who had less skin odor. Ae. albopictus was attracted to 13 chemicals that smell like plants. The different preferences suggest each species might have evolved its own way of finding a meal.

Many things could have influenced this, says Alicia Showering. These might include which animal hosts each species feeds on or what time of day the mosquitoes look for food. Showering runs BugBiome, a company based in Norwich, England. It develops insecticides from microbes that live on plants.

Human odor is very complex. That makes it difficult to detect every chemical in it, says Maria Elena De Obaldia. So there might be other attractive compounds the scientists didn’t turn up here, she says. In the past, De Obaldia has studied mosquitoes’ attraction to human scents. Now she works at Regeneron Pharmaceuticals. That’s a drug company in Tarrytown, N.Y. (Regeneron is a major financial supporter of the Society for Science, which publishes Science News Explores.)
iFhttps://www.sciencenews.org/conversion/zephr-iframe-test

Microbes produce many of the chemicals that make up our scent. So DeGennaro’s team also swabbed each volunteer’s skin for some of the bacteria living on it. Certain of these bacteria were attractive to all three species, they found.

The team now wants to focus on these skin bacteria, says Kaylee Marrero. She studies mosquito behavior at Florida International University and was the new study’s lead author. Her group wants to learn how skin bacteria make those smelly compounds that affect mosquitoes’ preferences. That might lead to microbe-based repellents. Or, Marrero adds, the most attractive chemicals could help design scented lures to bring mosquitoes into traps.
“We’re all trying to figure out how to stop people from getting sick,” Marrero says. “Figuring out why [mosquitoes] are biting people is the best way to do that.”

title: This ‘anti-vampiric’ grave was double guarded against the undead
content: *Partially_excavated_human_remains_have_a_sickle_blade_across_the_neck_Archaeological_markers_are_pla

Someone in post-medieval Poland seems to have feared this woman’s final resting place wouldn’t be so final. They placed this sickle over the neck of her corpse — perhaps so that she’d slit her throat if she attempted to rise from the grave.
Someone in 17th-century Poland really did not want one particular girl to rise from the dead.

In 2022, archaeologists unearthed an unsettling grave in Pień, part of north-central Poland. The young woman — who researchers call Zosia — had been buried in a cemetery there, with the jagged blade of a sickle hooked over her throat. Zosia also wore an odd triangular padlock on the big toe of her left foot.

“The placement of the sickle and the padlock suggests that the purpose of these practices was to protect the living from Zosia after her death,” says Dariusz Poliński. This included, “without a doubt, preventing her from rising from the grave.”

Poliński is an archaeologist at Nicolaus Copernicus University in Toruń, Poland. He led the excavation of Zosia’s final resting place. His team has now done a large set of analyses on the grave to piece together details of Zosia’s life and burial.
The group shared its findings in the October issue of Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports.
iFhttps://www.sciencenews.org/conversion/zephr-iframe-test

Poliński’s group first looked at other tombs in Europe where sickles and padlocks had been found. They also considered historical beliefs about such items. Both types of artifacts seem to have been used to shield the living from the dead, they found. But Zosia’s grave is the first known to have used both approaches.

Zosia’s skeleton suggests she was 17 to 19 years old when she died. Based on how her leg bones lay, the padlock was likely latched on her toe when she was first buried. This hints that someone suspected Zosia would try to rise from her grave right away.
*_This_‘anti-vampiric’_grave_was_double_guarded_against_the_undead_0
fCThis triangular padlock was latched onto the big toe of Zosia’s left foot.

On top of that, mixed-up soil and the odd angle of Zosia’s left arm suggest that someone later dug up her tomb. They likely did this to place the sickle over her throat, the researchers say. Someone wanted to be extra sure Zosia wouldn’t resurrect.

A close look at Zosia’s skull revealed greenish stains. The marks could have come from some copper object — or objects — being shoved in her mouth or nose. “This may have [been] an additional protective measure,” Poliński says. In Polish folklore, copper was thought to help ward off vampiric demons, known as strzygi.

Lauren Hosek has seen strange graves. But she doesn’t know if she’s seen stranger than this. A bioarchaeologist, she works at the University of Colorado Boulder and did not take part in this research.
A sickle across the neck is very striking, says Hosek. That, paired with the padlock as a restraint, offers a strong argument that this young woman was feared after her death.
Graves designed to fend off evil spirits are sometimes known as “anti-vampiric.” But that doesn’t necessarily mean that people in the 17th century thought Zosia was out for blood, Hosek cautions.
Today, we think of vampires as blood-sucking monsters associated with garlic and bats and capes. In this historical context, a vampire simply refers to some sort of harmful undead being.
To explain how a teen girl could have earned such anti-vampiric treatment, Poliński’s team analyzed the chemicals in her skeleton and accessories.

For instance, the team looked at the types — or isotopes — of strontium and oxygen atoms in her teeth. Dental isotopes hold clues about where someone lived during their childhood. Zosia’s show that she likely grew up near Pień. Her DNA, however, hints that her mother’s family might have come from Scandinavia.

Remnants of a silk cap on Zosia’s head contained threads of pure silver and gold. To be laid to rest in such fancy attire, the researchers think she must have been a wealthy woman of high social status.
*human_remains_in_a_shallow_excavated_grave_have_a_sickle_blade_placed_over_the_neck_and_a_lock_on_on
fCZosia’s grave is but one of several unusual burials in the Pień graveyard — maybe because the cemetery was specifically for people who were feared after their deaths.

Having so much information about someone entombed in an odd burial is rare, says Sandra Garvie-Lok. By knowing some details of Zosia’s life, this bioarchaeologist says, “we can rule out some commonly suggested explanations for this kind of [burial] treatment.” Garvie-Lok works at the University of Alberta in Edmonton, Canada. Like Hosek, she’s studied peculiar graves, but not this one.

Historical records have shown that someone might be singled out for a strange burial because they were an outsider or had a hard life, Garvie-Lok notes. But if Zosia was a noblewoman who grew up near Pień, then she may not neatly tick either of those boxes.

Violent or weird circumstances around her death might also account for Zosia’s strange burial. But there are no obvious marks of injury or illness on her skeleton. “We’re still looking at the DNA” for insights into how she died, says Tomasz Grzybowski. He’s a forensic geneticist at Nicolaus Copernicus University and coauthor of the new study.
The Pień cemetery is riddled with other eerie burials.

One boy there was buried face-down with a triangular padlock on his right foot. “Sometime later, the grave was reopened and most of his remains were removed,” Poliński says. This left “only the lower legs and feet in place, together with the padlock.”

Even spookier, there are no written references to this graveyard. It doesn’t appear on any maps. And because it was set away from the village, it may have been far from any church or chapel. All this points to the cemetery being specifically for people who had been rejected by society — and perhaps feared after their deaths.
If so, Garvie-Lok says, “this would make Pień a very unusual site that we could learn a lot from.”

title: Feeling nervous? Work that system to calm it down
content: *Close-up_of_a_woman_with_her_face_partly_submerged_in_water,_her_eyes_closed_beneath_the_surface

Cold water on the face seems to reduce the body’s stress responses to tough tasks. Scientists are studying this and other ways to help people regulate how their nervous system responds to stressful situations.

When you’re stressed, you lose some control. Stress hormones flood your bloodstream. Your heart rate and blood pressure go up. You breathe faster. These changes happen without thought. They’re run by what’s known as your sympathetic nervous system. And they kick in whether you’re facing true danger or just a big exam. But scientists are learning how to guide our nervous systems out of that fight-or-flight mode and into relaxation.

Some calming techniques come naturally. Maybe you’ve already used slow, deep breaths to recenter yourself. Now, though, there’s mounting data to support a range of zanier approaches. Ever tried humming, or tapping on your skin? What about dunking your face in cold water?

“Consciously, you can’t tell your heart to slow down,” explains Patricio Millar Vernetti. He’s a neurologist at NYU Langone Health in New York City. “But by doing these interventions, you have a little bit more control.”

On social media, these practices are often described as ways to “regulate” your nervous system. But it’s really about balancing two branches of your nervous system. That “sympathetic” branch is in charge of stress responses. It gets you ready for action, pumping blood to your brain and muscles. Its counterpart — the parasympathetic nervous system — calms things down.
Getting that parasympathetic nervous system to kick in can help calm us back to a resting state. It lowers stress hormone levels. It slows the heart and lowers blood pressure.

Being able to control this back-and-forth may yield big health benefits. Over time, an over-active stress response can contribute to a range of problems. These include high blood pressure, strain on the heart, inflammation and other issues.
These systems normally work without our giving them thought. But research is finding ways to turn on the parasympathetic nervous system when we feel it’s needed.
iFhttps://www.sciencenews.org/conversion/zephr-iframe-test

Stimulating the vagus nerve is one way. This nerve runs from the base of the brain (or brain stem) to the abdomen. Breathing exercises can fire up this nerve. So might cold therapy, research suggests.

In one small study, scientists observed 25 people doing math in their heads. Before this, 12 participants had worn a face-cooling mask. It was meant to mimic submerging their face in cold water; that’s a known way to stimulate the vagus nerve.

Everyone got stressed by the math task. But those who had first worn cooling masks didn’t release as much cortisol. It’s a stress hormone. These recruits also recovered from their stress faster. The researchers shared their findings several years ago in Scientific Reports.

Humming may also turn on the parasympathetic nervous system. In October 2025, for instance, scientists showed slow breathing plus humming can boost heart-rate variability. It’s a measure of the fluctuating time between heartbeats. That humming finding appeared in Physiology & Behavior.

High heart-rate variability is one sign of a well-regulated nervous system. It signals “your body is doing less fighting itself on the inside,” explains physical therapist Karin Steere. It’s now better able to switch between stress and relaxation. Steere works at the University of Puget Sound in Tacoma, Wash.
iFhttps://www.youtube.com/embed/Y_8mR_SsUnw?feature=oembed
fCCleveland Clinic/YouTube

Tapping on specific spots on the skin has also been shown to lower stress-hormone levels. It can also reduce heart rate and blood pressure. Tapping is even used as a type of therapy for some conditions, such as post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). Science is still exploring why this method works. A 2025 review suggests those taps may send signals to the brain that tell the parasympathetic nervous system it’s time to take over.

When it comes to regulating your nervous system, there’s really no one best way, says Darshan Mehta. He works at the Benson-Henry Institute for Mind Body Medicine. It’s part of Massachusetts General Hospital in Boston. It’s possible to find small, one-off studies that support nearly every viral technique you see, he notes. The most important thing, he says, is to find what works for you and stick to it.
“It’s not important which practice [people adopt],” Mehta says. What’s important, he adds, is “that people do practice [it].”

Some of these habits, Vernetti notes, have been in use a long time. Chanting and humming, for instance, are part of some ancient spiritual practices. “This is one of those things that science has caught up with relatively recently,” he says. In fact, “people have been doing [them] for centuries.”

title: Scientists Say: Blood Falls
content: *a_glacier_in_Antarctica_stained_dark_red

Red water flows out of cracks in this Antarctic glacier. For decades, scientists have wondered how this iron-rich water got here. A recent study suggests the lake underneath the glacier was filled in by the ocean millions of years ago.

iFhttps://w.soundcloud.com/player/?url=https%3A//api.soundcloud.com/tracks/soundcloud%253Atracks%253A2418995766&color=%23ff5500&auto_play=false&hide_related=false&show_comments=true&show_user=true&show_reposts=false&show_teaser=true

Blood Falls is a five-story waterfall that flows out of Taylor Glacier in Antarctica. The water comes from a salty lake beneath the glacier that’s rich in iron. When the water reaches the glacier’s surface, the iron interacts with oxygen in the air. This reaction turns the water red. It’s the same reaction that creates reddish rust on a nail.

Scientists suspect the lake was filled by ocean water 5 million years ago. But it’s been completely cut off from other water sources for at least a million years. Over time, the water became saltier as the glacier formed above. Now, the lake is more than twice as salty as the ocean. The water can’t freeze because salt prevents water molecules from locking into the crystal structure of ice.

Because the lake is also cut off from the atmosphere, scientists call it a biological time capsule. Microbes have lived here for millions of years with no light or oxygen. Instead, these extremophiles get their energy from molecules called sulfates. This respiration strategy is similar to microbes that live in deep-sea thermal vents.

But the Blood Falls microbes are special. They extract oxygen from the sulfates and leave behind other molecules. When these leftovers interact with iron in the water, they turn back into sulfates. This means these microbes have a practically unlimited energy source.

Scientists suspect planets like Mars and Jupiter’s icy moons could be home to salty underground lakes like this one. How these microbes make a living might be a clue for how life could work on other planets, too.
Blood Falls is located in East Antarctica, more than 3,300 kilometers (2,000 miles) south of New Zealand.

title: 2026’s El Niño is record-breaking — and it’s not done yet
content: *A_red_slash_that_reaches_from_the_mid_Pacific_Ocean_to_South_America,_along_with_other_hot_spots_alo
The strengthening of this year’s El Niño is creating a slash of warmer-than-normal sea-surface temperatures across the Pacific Ocean, seen here as a red-orange band on August 25.

Since June, scientists have been warning that Earth might experience an El Niño unlike any other. It now appears they were right. The periodic climate beast that emerged this year is stronger than any ever seen. And the really worrisome news: It likely hasn’t even reached its peak.

El Niños develop in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean. Over a short period, they release extraordinary amounts of ocean heat into the air. And by September 21, the daily sea-surface temperature where El Niños form was already 3.08 degrees Celsius (5.54 degrees Fahrenheit) warmer than the average from 1991 to 2020.

El Niños can fuel droughts, floods, heat waves and severe storms. The Oceanic Niño Index is a traditional measurement of their strength. Using daily sea-surface temperatures to calculate strength shows that the 2026 event is already more intense than any in recorded history.

“It has been a remarkable event,” says Nathaniel Johnson. What’s more, the climate scientist notes, this El Niño will probably strengthen even more. He expects it to peak “within the next few months.” Johnson works at the Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory in Princeton, N.J. It’s part of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).

Ocean heat released by this El Niño could spike global land temperatures about 1.2 degrees C (2.16 degrees F) in the coming months. That may not sound like much. But by next February, it could lead to more than 450,000 additional heat-related deaths. That’s the finding of a new report out of the University of Chicago’s Climate Impact Lab.

NOAA has not yet formally called this El Niño a record-breaker. Why? It’s using a new measurement method: the Relative Oceanic Niño index. That should better capture how an El Niño’s heat will alter weather across the globe. And by this index, the El Niño in 1997 and 1998 topped the new one’s current strength.
*A_group_of_men_pulling_a_horse_burdened_with_bags_through_flood_water,_behind_them_another_man_on_a_

fCWhat was one of the strongest recent El Niños developed during 1997 and 1998. One impact: It flooded large regions of Ecuador, in South America. Here in the Guayaquil region, for instance, flooding forced thousands of people out of their homes and cut off most roadways.
But that record, too, is on track to be broken soon, based on a Sept. 10 forecast by NOAA’s Climate Prediction Center.

To understand what’s driving this historic event and its potential impacts, Science News spoke with two experts. One is Johnson, part of that U.S. team that produces El Niño forecasts. The other, Nathan Lenssen, is a climate scientist at the National Center of Atmospheric Research. It’s in Boulder, Colo. Their answers have been edited for length and clarity.

Johnson: It’s really an unanswered question. If we look at the historical record, we have been seeing more rapid swings between El Niño and La Niña. [La Niña is the other — and opposite — extreme phase of a seesawing pair of climate patterns: Together they’re known as ENSO, or the El Niño Southern Oscillation.] There’s some evidence from computer models that increasing greenhouse-gas emissions lead to more of those extreme [ENSO] swings. But there’s no science consensus yet on how climate change is impacting El Niño. Especially an extreme one, like this.

Lenssen: There’s debate on how much we can directly attribute to climate change. But due to Earth’s warming, there is more energy in the oceans now. And El Niños release some of that ocean heat into the atmosphere.
iFhttps://www.youtube.com/embed/WPA-KpldDVc?start=21&feature=oembed
Learn how changes in the equatorial Pacific Ocean can trigger an El Niño. Then watch where and how in coming months those changes may dramatically alter weather patterns elsewhere across the planet.

Johnson: We see a lot of the most predictable impacts in the tropics. That’s where an El Niño develops. We’ve already seen a suppressed Atlantic hurricane season and enhanced Pacific hurricane season. We’ve also seen droughts in Central America. We tend to see droughts over northern South America and the Amazon. Meanwhile, the Indian monsoon can weaken.

By late fall, we typically see more impacts a bit farther from the equator. For instance, we tend to see more rain over the southern United States, but it’s typically drier than normal over the Pacific Northwest. And it’ll be warmer than average over the northern United States and Canada.

Lenssen: While this El Niño is quite powerful, that doesn’t necessarily mean we’re more confident about its impacts. A global warming of the oceans has made some historical changes seen at mid-latitudes less likely.

So there’s a kind of twist there. The El Niño in 2023 and 2024, for instance, didn’t lead to as much wet weather in California as expected. And some research has shown that was due to other warming ocean patterns.

Johnson: El Niños typically last a year. So we’ll probably see this one weaken after winter and be over by spring or early summer. But when we have a big El Niño like this, we’re more likely to see a shift in the following year to La Niña [which also has global impacts on weather]. So that’s something we’ll be keeping our eye on.

Lenssen: It’s possible that this event could be followed by a double La Niña. Those occur back-to-back, separated by a brief period of neutral conditions. That happened in 2016 and 2017, after the strong El Niño of 2014 and 2015.

Johnson: We’ve seen such a dramatic change in the equatorial Pacific Ocean. The move has been very rapid, from a La Niña last winter to a very strong El Niño — all in less than a year. That might be the fastest transition that we’ve seen.

Lenssen: Though more work is needed to understand this, some research suggests future El Niños may actually become more predictable as the world continues to warm. That might give us months of additional lead time to prepare for their impacts. And that would be great.

Since El Niño emerged in June, the daily average sea-surface temperature has become extraordinarily high in the heart of the Pacific Ocean region where El Niños develop. On September 21, it reached 3.08 degrees Celsius (5.54 degrees Fahrenheit) above both the 1991 to 2020 average (coarse dashed line) and the 1982 to 2010 average (fine dashed line). Prior to September 2026, the most extreme anomaly on record was 3.02 degrees Celsius, set by an El Niño in November 2015.

title: Newfound clouds of missing ‘ordinary’ matter sit outside galaxies
content: *an_image_of_deep_space_showing_hundreds_thousands_of_galaxies

This image of deep space, taken by the Hubble Space Telescope, shows countless galaxies. Tiny flashes of radio waves from far away pass through gases extending from galaxies like these. Those radio waves have now illuminated where some of the universe’s “missing” matter may be lurking.

For years, scientists have been calculating how much matter should exist in our universe. But more than half of it didn’t appear to be showing up in telescope images. Now an explanation for why is emerging. The “missing” matter is just too diffuse — or spread out — to see. Some of it may not even be made of complete atoms.

“The missing matter exists as a thin gas that’s very spread out,” says Haochen Wang. Wang works at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in Cambridge. A PhD student in astrophysics, he led the new study. Think of the missing matter, he says, as faint clouds. They’re huge, stretching far beyond the edges of galaxies.

This missing matter is considered ordinary. By that, scientists mean it’s made of everyday particles called baryons. Those include the protons and neutrons that make up stars, planets and people. Ordinary matter is quite different from another type of unseen stuff called “dark matter.” That’s a mysterious substance that doesn’t emit, reflect or absorb light at all. (Scientists only know it’s there because its gravity pulls on other things.)

In some spots, Wang says, the unseen ordinary matter is so spread out that there’s less than one proton or electron in a space about the size of a washing machine. That, he explains, is why finding it has proven “such a hard puzzle to solve.”
iFhttps://www.sciencenews.org/conversion/zephr-iframe-test

To find this diffuse matter, Wang’s group focused on fast radio bursts, or FRBs. Each of these very intense bursts of radio waves lasts about one-thousandth of a second. They flare up somewhere in the far-off universe, then vanish.
As an FRB races toward Earth, it passes through the gas floating between galaxies. That gas, the missing matter, stretches out an FRB’s radio light, Wang explains.

This separates a distant FRB’s light into distinct wavelengths. It’s a bit similar to the way a prism splits white light into a rainbow. When radio waves travel through gas, those with longer wavelengths move more slowly than shorter-wavelength ones. And the difference in their speed grows ever larger as FRBs travel through more matter.

Overall, that change in speed still “is a really small effect,” says astrophysicist Liam Connor. He works at Harvard University in Cambridge, Mass. But “over billions of years of traveling through this … matter, it becomes a detectable effect here on Earth.”

Telescopes pick up a stretched-out signal, where short-wavelength radio waves arrive first, and longer wavelengths trail behind. “The more missing matter the signal goes through,” Connor says, “the more stretched it gets.”
The new findings appear in the July Physical Review Letters.
*two_maps_showing_where_fast_radio_bursts_have_been_located_in_a_sky_map

fCThe upper map shows where fast radio bursts have been spotted across the sky. The lower map shows how galaxies are spread across the sky. The new study found a significant correlation between the two maps. The comparison turned up formerly missing “ordinary” matter in our universe.

Connor is part of a different team that’s been searching for the missing matter. Last year, his group measured how much each FRB reaching Earth had stretched. The scientists did this by comparing FRB data to a computer model.

This allowed the team to calculate how much gas the radio waves had passed through. It also pointed to roughly where that gas was. A 2025 study in Nature Astronomy estimated how much missing matter sits between, around and inside galaxies.

Also last year, another team directly detected one specific filament of hot gas. It linked several galaxy clusters and is thought to contain some of the missing ordinary matter. The team, led by Konstantinos Migkas at Leiden University in the Netherlands, used X-rays rather than FRBs to find this gas.
Submit your question here, and we might answer it an upcoming issue of Science News Explores

Now Wang’s team has directly measured how far gas typically stretches around galaxies. Unlike Connor’s group, they did this without leaning on a computer model to fill in the picture. They say it’s the first definitive detection of the missing ordinary matter.

Vikram Ravi is hesitant to call it the first. An astronomer, Ravi works at the California Institute of Technology in Pasadena. Connor’s 2025 work, he says, at least hinted the gas was out there — even if no one had directly measured its reach. Ravi also points out that some of the new study’s numbers could be off, if the FRBs’ distances weren’t measured precisely enough.
Still, he considers the latest work “a great signpost of what is to come.”
*an_image_showing_diffuse_matter_as_clouds_of_gas_spread_out_around_galaxies

fC This image shows a model of how diffuse gas (colored blue, green and yellow) is spread around galaxies (white dots on the image). A new study reports that this gas extends much farther out from galaxies than earlier research had suggested.

Wang’s group studied 2,870 FRBs. All had been detected by the CHIME radio telescope in British Columbia, Canada. The team compared these bursts to the known locations of nearly 6 million galaxies. The galaxies had been mapped by the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument, or DESI. It sits atop Manzanita Shrub Mountain in Arizona.
To identify where the missing gas is, the researchers lined up each stretched-out FRB across the galaxy map.

The gas doesn’t cling tightly to galaxies the way gravity alone might suggest. Instead, the diffuse matter puffs outward in thin clouds. Some clouds extend roughly 4 million light-years beyond a galaxy’s edge. That’s much farther than most computer models had predicted.

“Just like fountains that can spout water, there must be activities in galaxies that can push gas out to a large distance, despite gravity’s pull,” Wang says. What might they be? Perhaps jets, he says, that black holes blast out as they’re feeding. Or maybe they’re supernovas, explosions from dying stars. Whatever the sources, they’re exerting more force than scientists had suspected.

Victoria Kaspi is a physicist at McGill University in Montreal, Canada, who worked with Wang on the new study. She thinks their approach to mapping diffuse matter could change how astronomers study the universe. FRBs, she says, “are amazingly effective” in probing how matter is distributed across the cosmos.

Knowing where ordinary matter hides is important. Astronomers map it to understand how galaxies form, evolve and interact with their environment. They also use these matter maps in their search for other unknown phenomena, such as dark energy and dark matter (which is believed to make up the vast majority of our universe).
If the “normal” matter map is wrong, these bigger puzzles get even harder to solve.
The new study is “an exciting and impressive work,” says Connor. “I think it’s a sign of good things to come for the application of FRBs to mapping the cosmic baryons.”
New radio telescopes are also being built. They should be able to pinpoint FRBs far more precisely. In the coming years, these telescopes could boost the number of recorded FRBs 100 times or more.
Ravi’s team, among others, is already preparing to use larger FRB catalogs in hopes of making even sharper maps of cosmic gas.
“The more FRBs we find,” Wang says, “the more accurate our answers on the missing matter will become. That includes the powerful galactic forces shaping it.”

title: These clues might point to life on other worlds
content: *the_planet_Mars_against_a_black_background
A microbe that normally lives in sewage sludge and muddy lake bottoms might be able to survive on Mars.

Lead-melting temperatures on the surface of Venus should make life as we know it impossible there. But scientists have detected some curious chemicals in clouds above the planet’s surface. At those heights, temps and pressures would be similar to those on Earth.

These clouds sit 48 to 60 kilometers (30 to 37 miles) above the surface. Potential traces of oxygen, methane and phosphine gas have shown up in them. This has led some scientists to suspect the clouds might host microbes. But those single-celled life forms would have to survive harsh conditions when they occasionally sank into lower, hotter layers of the atmosphere.

In 2021, researchers at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, in Cambridge, suggested how microbes might survive in clouds high above Venus. They would just need to tolerate briefly drying out whenever they sank into hotter cloud layers. Later, when swept back into cooler, wetter layers, the cells could revive. Noelle Bryan, Sara Seager and their colleagues proposed this idea.
*an_image_of_the_planet_Venus_against_a_black_background,_showing_swirling_light-colored_clouds

fCNASA’s first close-up of the swirling clouds that obscure the surface of Venus. It was taken by the Mariner 10 on Feb. 5, 1974. Scientists have recently found that those clouds contain the chemical signatures of gas that might have been made by microbial life.

Bryan had reasons for thinking this might be possible. Years before, she had collected microbes from Earth’s stratosphere. This hostile zone sits dozens of kilometers (miles) above our planet’s surface. The microbes she found seemed to survive extreme drying while up there — much as the Venus microbes would have to survive drying out.
What Bryan learned about those high-flying cells might now guide the search for alien life in solar systems light-years away.

For instance, some bacteria on Earth produce colorful pigments. These molecules can protect the cells from harmful ultraviolet (UV) radiation. Finding them on other worlds might point to life there. Extraterrestrial cells might use similar pigments to protect themselves from UV too.

Future telescopes looking at planets orbiting distant stars might be able to detect the colors of those pigments. This could reveal microbial life living in the clouds of faraway worlds, says Lígia Coelho. An astrobiologist, she works at Cornell University in Ithaca, N.Y.

Coelho recently analyzed pigments in Bryan’s stratospheric bacteria. The pigments absorbed or reflected specific wavelengths of light, she found. She hopes to look for similar light and color patterns in distant planets.
iFhttps://www.youtube.com/embed/kCuJvBQPpas?feature=oembed
Lindsay Hays, a NASA program scientist, describes what researchers mean when they talk about looking for a “biosignature” of life, especially extraterrestrial life.

The recent discovery of microbes in Earth’s stratosphere is probably most relevant to imagining life on Mars. After all, cells high above Earth endure conditions similar to those on the Red Planet’s surface.

Andrew Schuerger has spent years hunting Earthly microbes that might be able to survive on Mars. He works at the University of Florida in Gainesville. He recently teamed up with Rachel Harris. She’s an astrobiologist at NASA and Harvard University in Cambridge, Mass. Last year, the duo found a microbe that seems to check many of the boxes needed to make it on Mars.
Its name is a mouthful: Methanosarcina barkeri (Meh-THAAN-oh-sar-SEE-nuh BARK-er-eye). It gets its energy by turning carbon dioxide and hydrogen into methane.

M. barkeri normally lives in sewage, landfills, rice paddies and lake bottoms. Those buried habitats would hardly mimic Mars’ thin, dry air. But unlike microbes in Earth’s stratosphere, M. barkeri can live without oxygen, which is absent on Mars. And even at low, Mars-like pressures, M. barkeri can still make methane, Schuerger and Harris have shown.
iFhttps://www.sciencenews.org/conversion/zephr-iframe-test
That’s big news, because Mars orbiters and rovers have detected methane gas seeping into Mars’ atmosphere.
Unfortunately, methane-making critters on Mars would likely be hard to spot. They might need to hide deep underground to survive the planet’s low atmospheric pressure.

But finding that M. barkeri is active at low pressures means life might be able to survive quite close to the Red Planet’s surface, Schuerger says. A rover might only need to drill 20 centimeters (8 inches) down to reach single-celled Martians — if they exist.
iFhttps://www.youtube.com/embed/iIJcqiqYXG8?feature=oembed
NASA rovers are scouting rocks on the Martian surface. They hope to confirm potential signs that this planet once hosted life — even if that life was only one-celled microbes.

Any pockets of microbes near Mars’ surface might be quite small and short-lived, says Lynn Rothschild. She’s an astrobiologist at NASA Ames Research Center. It’s in Mountain View, Calif. She imagines microbes using Mars’ surface the way high-flying species seem to use Earth’s stratosphere. It would be a hostile place they briefly tolerate while moving from one home to another.

If she’s right, then windstorms on Mars might sweep up not only dust, but also Martian life. Microbes could be “floating around, just looking for a place to land [where] they can survive” and grow, she says. If so, then a rover might catch life the way a fence catches blowing leaves.
*an_animated_photo_showing_a_selfie_taken_by_the_Mars_Rover_Perseverance_in_a_site_that_may_have_show

fCNASA’s Perseverance rover took a selfie on the surface of Mars. In 2024, it came to this site, nicknamed Cheyava Falls, where it detected signs of past water, organic material and more. Last year, researchers published a study suggesting that this site might once have hosted life.

title: Is AI making us dumber? Depends how it’s used
content: *an_illustration_of_a_person_with_information_blooming_out_of_their_brain
Our learned skills can fade if we rely too much on AI, scientists say. To keep skills or learn new ones, we need to keep our brains engaged.

AI today can write our class essays, plan our meals and draft our emails. But not everyone agrees on whether this type of help is good or bad. Recent headlines have warned that artificial intelligence will not just make us lazy and stupid; they’ve suggested AI could lead to the downfall of civilization. But the truth may lie somewhere in the middle of those best- and worst-case scenarios, says Trent Cash. He’s a behavioral scientist at University of Waterloo in Canada.
The type of AI tool and how it’s used make all the difference in whether someone hangs onto or picks up skills, new data show.

AI will most likely weaken our skills when it simply does the work for us. “If we offload a specific skill to AI,” Cash says, “we’re probably not going to retain that skill particularly well.” Staying engaged while using AI — by learning from its feedback or examples — may, however, enhance our skills.
Fears of AI whittling away human intelligence like some sort of digital pocketknife are likely overblown, Cash says. He dismisses the idea that AI will cause people to completely forget how to think.
“Humans are resilient,” he points out. “I don’t think that [AI is] going to suddenly turn our brains to mush.” But staying sharp will take effort on our part.
iFhttps://www.sciencenews.org/conversion/zephr-iframe-test
A new wave of research is sketching out how our brains deal with help from AI. The answer can sometimes look grim.

Take one 2025 study of doctors who’d been trained to spot growths — called polyps — on patients’ colons. Doctors got an AI tool’s help spotting polyps for three months. Later, when the doctors returned to working alone, they didn’t detect polyps as well. This suggests the doctors “kind of forgot what to look for,” Cash says.

The same pattern plays out with other skills, such as learning a new math concept. One 2025 study looked at high-school students using an AI tool like ChatGPT to solve practice problems. The AI seemed to help. But take the tool away, and those students did worse than ones who never used it.

Something similar can happen with reading comprehension. Consider people who used an AI tool to solve practice SAT questions. Those people had a hard time coming up with correct answers when the AI was taken away, a new study finds. After losing their AI helper, people were also more likely to skip questions.
*a_top_down_view_of_a_girl_with_dark_hair_sitting_at_a_desk_studying,_she_has_a_notebook_full_of_high

fCMore than half of U.S. teens use chatbots for homework. Treating AI like a tutor may help them pick up new skills. But turning to AI to simply churn out answers is unlikely to result in real learning.

That was “particularly concerning,” the study’s authors conclude, because persistence is key for learning. These researchers shared the findings at the 2026 Conference on Language Modeling in San Francisco, Calif., on October 8.
All these results suggest people can struggle once they let AI take over their tasks.

For Cash, the lesson is “use it or lose it” — where “it” is your own brainpower. Don’t let AI do all your thinking for you, he says. “If you’re not engaging with the cognitive work, you’re not going to learn the skill.”

Using AI doesn’t have to mean your skills will crumble. You can put in the effort needed to learn even as you’re getting digital help, says Alp Sungu. The key is using AI tools that offer guidance or examples, rather than spitting out answers.

Sungu is an economist at the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia. He worked on the study of high-school students using AI for math. In that study, his team designed an AI tool with some limits. It worked like ChatGPT but didn’t give away answers. Instead, it offered hints and encouragement. That approach helped students learn as well as those who just studied with books.

Using AI as a tutor is different from using it as an answer machine, Sungu says. Students still had to put thought into their studying. The struggle of working through a new concept is where real learning happens, he says. “When you’re solving a problem, you need to get your hands dirty.”
For those willing to put in some effort, AI can be a good teacher, says Benjamin Lira Luttges. This behavioral scientist also works at the University of Pennsylvania.

An AI tool can help people learn how to edit cover letters, his research has shown. After practicing with either an AI tool or human feedback, people edited a poorly written cover letter without any help. Then, human judges picked which letters would likely land a job interview. Letters from both groups were equally likely to get picked, Lira Luttges’ group reports. The team shared these results on arxiv.org in February. (Studies posted there have not yet been vetted by other scientists.)

The AI tool in that study had taught by rewriting an entire cover letter itself. That may sound like its students weren’t doing much thinking. But it’s not what the team found. People didn’t just accept the AI-revised draft. They sat with it for a while, tinkering with the language. “They were still working,” Lira Luttges says.
*an_illustration_of_a_man_standing_at_a_computer_and_chatting_with_a_robot_standing_next_to_him_that_
fCAI can help us learn new skills when it offers guidance rather than simply spitting out answers.
This hints that AI can teach by example — “if you have people who are motivated to learn,” he says. In short, AI systems that keep people’s brains engaged might be able to sharpen some of our skills.

Still, we should be careful in choosing what thinking we outsource to computers, experts say. If there’s a skill you value, don’t give it over to AI, Cash advises. “We know skills come from practice and are maintained through practice.”

Lira Luttges agrees. People should think about what skills they want to protect, he says. That might be coming up with the perfect way to phrase a sentence. Or it may be devising a tasty dish using items in your pantry.
“You shouldn’t delegate the things that you enjoy and that give you meaning,” he says. “Outsource the crap, not the craft.”

title: Let’s learn about origami-inspired science
content: *a_red,_blue_and_yellow_paper_origami_crane
The Japanese art of paper folding is called origami — from the Japanese words “oru” (to fold) and “kami” (paper).

People have used origami for centuries to transform flat pieces of paper into 2-D and 3-D shapes. In minutes, a beginner can use this Japanese art of paper folding to craft simple birds, flowers and jumping frogs. More advanced patterns can give rise to highly detailed sculptures of all manner of objects.
Scientists have used geometry, algebra and other branches of math to invent new origami designs. Such designs can not only be used to create art. They can lead to new compact and shapeshifting tech.

Take the James Webb Space Telescope, the biggest telescope ever sent to space. It’s so big that it had to be folded up origami-style to fit in a rocket. Engineers have also used origami techniques to make robots that can squeeze through tight spaces. And bots that change shape to do different tasks or move in precise ways to handle fragile objects.

Kirigami, a related art form that combines paper folding and cutting, has also inspired engineers. Some have used this Japanese art to design shoe soles that change shape to increase grip. Others have built kirigami parachutes that automatically open when dropped.

Teen paper folders are pushing this field forward, too. One middle-school student in New York City recently discovered that a certain type of origami fold could support 9,000 times its own weight. That might make it useful for designing pop-up emergency shelters. And a high-schooler in Japan came up with a new way to model complex folds, like those found in origami and ladybug wings. His advance could help engineers build new nature-inspired tech.

title: Explainer: What is an equation?
content: *a_girl_with_dark_curly_hair_writes_an_equation_on_a_whiteboard
There are several ways to write a multiplication problem. This young girl is attempting to answer one that has been displayed linearly — as an equation.

An equation is a mathematical statement that’s written linearly — in a straight line. It has two parts separated by an equal sign (=). And as that sign would suggest, what appears on either side of it has the exact same value.
*Text_One_example_5_x_4_=_20

Math statements weren’t always written this way. Even today, grade-school kids learn to write these statements vertically — with numbers above and below a straight line. That line corresponds to the equal sign. For instance:
*5_x_4_=_20,_written_vertically
One might be tempted to think that equations as we know them are as old as math. But no. Math goes back millennia. The symbols used in equations are relatively recent.

Centuries ago, “math used to be written out” in words, notes British mathematician Robin Wilson. “They call it rhetorical algebra.” A math historian, he authored the 2025 book, Sum Stories: Equations and Their Origins. People used to use regular words to express additions, subtractions and other relationships between numbers and the things they were counting.
*a_photo_of_a_carving_memorializing_Robert_Recorde_showing_his_face
fCRobert Recorde, a 16th-century Welsh mathematician, made equations possible by inventing the “equal to” symbol.

For instance, someone might have written: “Ship one brought two hundred fish to port. Fifty were flounder, seventy-five were bream, twenty-seven were sharks and forty-eight were anchovies.” Now it might be shortened to 50 flounder + 75 bream + 27 sharks + 48 anchovies = 200 fish.

But that shortened version couldn’t have been written before 1557. That’s when the equal sign made its world debut in The Whetstone of Witte. (This math book’s name literally means sharpening your wits). Its author was Welsh mathematician Robert Recorde.

Among many things in this tome, Recorde introduces that equal symbol so he can avoid having to tediously repeat the words “is equal to.” Why choose two horizontal lines of the same length? Because, he argued, no two things can be more equal. (Of course, he said it a bit differently, as he was writing it in a very early version of modern English.)
That equal sign was a relative latecomer among our familiar math symbols. People started using the plus (+) and minus (-) signs around the late 1300s and early 1400s.
*a_photo_of_the_The_first_known_definition_and_use_of_“equal_to”_symbol_as_it_appeared_in_the_1557_bo

fCThe first known definition — and use of “equal to” symbol (14x + 15 = 71) — appears in the 1557 book, The Whetstone of Witte (written in Early Modern English). It includes the phrase: “[T]o avoid the tedious repetition of … ‘is equal to’ I will set … a pair of … [twin] lines of one length, thus: =====, because no 2 things can be more equal.”

And the equation at the start of this piece would have made no sense before 1631. That’s when William Oughtred, a 17th-century English math expert, introduced the “x” mark for multiplication (in his book Clavis Mathematicae).

“The equal sign is quite interesting and is slightly different from an operator like plus, minus, divide or multiply,” says Clemency Montelle. She’s a math historian at the University of Canterbury, New Zealand. The equal sign, she notes, “is not saying calculate anything. But it is indicating a relationship: that one thing on one side is identical [to the other side].”
And that’s true, she notes, “even if they don’t look the same.”
In 4+1 = 5, the two digits on the left-hand side don’t look identical to the digit on the right. Still, they have the exact same value. Montelle finds this quite a “powerful” idea.

“Equations are a way of expressing what you’re doing accurately, precisely and efficiently,” Wilson adds. The “=” signifies a balance — like on a scale — between the quantities on the left and right sides.
iFhttps://www.sciencenews.org/conversion/zephr-iframe-test

Knowing that there’s a balance between the mathematical expressions on either side of an equal sign allows us to solve for something in that expression that may be unknown. This is the basis of algebra, an especially useful branch of math.

Suppose we know that Daniel and Alice picked 9 apples from their backyard tree. We know that Daniel has 5 apples. Given this information, we can calculate how many Alice has. It can be written as this hybrid word problem:
*Text_5_+_unknown_quantity_=_9
By subtracting 5 from each side, we can calculate that the unknown quantity — the number of apples Alice has — must be 4.
Here the unknown quantity was apples. But it could be anything. Mathematicians generally refer to such an unknown with a letter. Often it’s an “x”.

Earlier in history, some cultures used other approaches. The ancient Indians, for instance, used word abbreviations for various colors to represent some unknown values. Ancient Mesopotamians used different words that meant such things as length, width and area to denote some unknowns.
iFhttps://www.youtube.com/embed/m0LzR5BqmHE?feature=oembed
fCHouse of Math/YouTube
Being able to calculate an unknown number makes equations widely useful.

Before equations existed, ancient astronomers painstakingly developed tables of numbers. Think of multiplication tables, with the numbers to be multiplied in the first row and column and the products of those multiplications filling in the rest of the table. This allows anyone to read out the answer for any product quickly.

Similarly, astronomers used tables to track a planet’s motion, observe phases of the moon and predict eclipses. If they wanted to follow a planet’s motion, they’d go down the table to the day and look across to read the number. Such a table could span weeks, months or even years. Creating them took painstaking amounts of mathematical effort.
Submit your question here, and we might answer it an upcoming issue of Science News Explores

Equations offer a compact substitute for such tables. Each equation describes the relationship between features of interest, such as a planet’s motion over time. To use it, you input the known values into the equation. For instance, this might be the date and the planet’s position. Then by performing the operations in that equation, you can calculate some unknown value, such as the distance traveled by the planet.
“Equations might seem rather dry,” says Montelle. “But they reveal a hidden structure or numerical pattern that we would otherwise have to write out one by one by one.”
That’s why behind the scenes, equations now play important roles throughout society.

They help engineers design and construct safer buildings. They can let airline pilots calculate how much fuel they’ll need if they know the distance they’re traveling and average speed they’ll be flying. And suppose you have a cake recipe that calls for 2.75 cups of flour. You could use an equation to scale up or down the ingredients needed to make one that’s two and a half times as big or just a mini-cake one-quarter the normal size.

title: Let’s learn about hydrogels
content: *_Let’s_learn_about_hydrogels1
Hydrogels are polymer-based materials sop up water like sponges — and can later release it for a variety of uses.
What do Jell-O, contact lenses and 3-D printed body parts have in common?
They all rely on hydrogels.

Hydrogels are polymer-based materials that can absorb and release lots of water. These materials are composed of threadlike molecules tangled in a complex mesh. That netting easily snags water, or H2O, molecules.

Some hydrogels are made of natural polymers. Jell-O is a good example. It contains a natural polymer called gelatin. Other hydrogels are made with synthetic polymers — and can be put to work in many different ways.

Some hydrogels can suck moisture out of the air and release it for drinking water. Others can collect H2O from dirty water while leaving pollutants behind. Hydrogels can even be added to soil. When someone waters their crops, those hydrogels soak up the moisture and release it slowly. That keeps water from flowing or evaporating off the soil.

Hydrogels are especially useful for making stuff that must touch living tissue. That’s because hydrogels and living tissue are both mostly water. Hydrogels have been used to make contact lenses and medical implants. Some engineers have also used hydrogels to 3-D print human tissues for transplants. The bioinks used to print these tissues mix live cells with a hydrogel ooze that protects the cells.

title: Sliding down surfaces can make rainwater corrosive
content: *Vehicles_and_pedestrians_cross_the_Golden_Gate_Bridge_on_a_foggy_damp-looking_day
Metal structures like the Golden Gate Bridge, monuments and cars are vulnerable to corrosion, even when covered with protective coatings.

Raindrops may be doing untold damage to cars, bridges, monuments and other outdoor structures. Not all rain, new data show. Just droplets that have first picked up an electric charge. One way they can get that charge: sliding off other surfaces, such as leaves, glass or buildings.

Rain droplets can then transfer their charge to materials that have the right electrical properties. That includes metals. This eventually corrodes, or eats away, at the metals. And even metals treated with protective coatings can corrode, the new data show.
Researchers shared these findings in the September 10 Nature.

Scientists knew water droplets could wear down structures by pounding on them. Rains can also contain small amounts of corrosive compounds, such as acids. But it wasn’t clear whether electrified drops would cause damage, says physicist Zhongyuan Ni. He works at the Max Planck Institute for Polymer Research. It’s in Mainz, Germany.

In early experiments, Ni found no damage to a copper surface after it was pelted with hundreds of water droplets. But one day, he says, “I just let the experiment [keep] running.” He kind of forgot about it as he went “to drink coffee or something.” When he came back, the copper looked different. A co-worker suggested it might have been damaged in some way.
This spurred Ni’s team to investigate further.
iFhttps://www.sciencenews.org/conversion/zephr-iframe-test

His team continuously released drops of water onto Teflon-coated copper. Copper is more resistant to corrosion than many other metals. And Teflon is an especially strong, protective coating. If the drops started eating into this protected surface, they reasoned, charged raindrops could probably do it to other metals, too.

The researchers gave some drops an electric charge. They did this by having the water slide along leaves or construction materials. The team also tipped uncharged water drops directly onto the Teflon-coated copper.

When viewed under a microscope, all copper surfaces hit with electrically charged drops appeared damaged. The charged water had eaten through the Teflon and begun corroding the copper below. Uncharged water droplets triggered no such damage.
Similar effects appeared on samples of copper and gold covered in polystyrene glass — another protective coating. Clearly, charged water could wear through more than Teflon.

As water droplets slide down common surfaces — such as leaves and glass — they can pick up an electric charge. In a test setup (left), when thousands of these drops landed on Teflon-coated copper, they caused damage that could be seen under a microscope (bottom row; scale bar represents 100 micrometers).
*A_diagram_on_the_left_shows_how_a_drop_of_water_picks_up_an_electrical_charge_as_it_slides_down_a_ti
fCZ. Ni et al./Nature 2026
The new findings could pave the way for better anticorrosion coatings, says Stefan Weber. A physicist at the University of Stuttgart in Germany, he did not take part in the study.

Water drops can become charged in clouds or by sliding along your windshield. But they should not scare you, Ni says. Their effects are small. Still, they could add up when cars, ships, monuments and machinery are exposed to the elements for years.
Small charges shouldn’t be ignored, Ni says. Even if they’re tiny, “sometimes they will play an important role.”

title: Could Spider-Man really turn off his superpowers?
content: *Spider-Man_swings_through_skyscrapers_while_a_villain_below_him_throws_a_pair_of_silver_boomerangs_I
In Spider-Man: Brand New Day, the web-slinger builds a superpower inhibitor. It’s based on real science for treating diseases.
Note: Slight spoilers ahead for Spider-Man: Brand New Day.

In Spider-Man: Brand New Day, Peter Parker has disturbing symptoms caused by DNA from the spider bite that gave him superpowers. He’d like to get rid of some of his new features while keeping others. So he visits Bruce Banner to discuss a device Banner invented to keep his own alter-ego, the Hulk, in check. It’s a superpower inhibitor. And it’s based on actual treatments for diseases.
In one scene, Parker asks Banner how the inhibitor turns off the genes in his DNA that cause Banner to Hulk out. “You’re using target-specific short interfering RNA, right?” Parker asks.

That’s not just movie technobabble. Short interfering RNAs, or siRNAs, are real molecules. They can effectively “turn off” some of a person’s genes. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has approved at least eight siRNA treatments for genetic diseases. Others are in clinical trials. Parker builds a device that injects siRNAs to control his unwanted powers.

fCIn Spider-Man: Brand New Day, Peter Parker (played by Tom Holland) visits Bruce Banner (Mark Ruffalo). They discuss how Banner keeps his alter-ego, the Hulk, in check. That tech is the inspiration for the superpower inhibitor that Peter then builds.
siRNAs work by interrupting a cell’s chemical assembly line.
The instructions to build and maintain a living thing are housed in its DNA. And the pieces of DNA responsible for different traits are called genes.

To put a bit of DNA into action, a cell first makes copies of its chemical instructions. Those copies are known as messenger RNAs, or mRNAs. Other parts of the cell then read mRNA instructions to build proteins. Proteins are molecules that carry out various tasks inside a living thing.

Small interfering RNAs do their work in between the DNA-copying and protein-building steps. They can latch onto mRNAs carrying instructions from specific genes. That marks those mRNAs for destruction, and they get chopped up. The interference prevents proteins from being made from those mRNAs. It essentially silences the genes whose instructions the mRNAs had copied.
Some siRNAs occur naturally in cells. They help control protein production. But scientists have also designed siRNAs to silence genes that cause disease.

Shutting down foreign DNA — such as DNA from a spider — is the sort of thing siRNAs do well, says Anastasia Khvorova. She’s a chemical biologist at the University of Massachusetts Chan Medical School in Worcester.

If Spider-Man’s powers come from a single gene, then an siRNA targeting that gene could work, she says. But in the film, Parker wants to shut off several traits, such as making spiderweb silk and having painfully heightened senses. It’s rare for a single gene to control such different traits. So Parker would probably need to make a mix of different siRNAs to tackle all his new spider traits.

Plus, genes don’t work in isolation, says Khvorova. Shutting one down may affect others. In the movie, Banner warns that “it would be enormously dangerous and complex” to shut down some parts of Hulk but keep others.
*A_graphic_showing_how_RNA_interference_works_A_red_and_orange_strand_of_RNA_are_shown_twisted_togeth
fCAlnylam Pharmaceuticals

RNA interference, or RNAi, is one way cells control protein production. Molecules called small interfering RNAs enter the cell as a double-stranded pair (orange and red, left). Once in the cell, the siRNA enters a cellular machine called RISC. There, the two strands unzip. One strand (orange) pairs with a target messenger RNA, or mRNA, that carries instructions for making a specific protein. That pairing slates the mRNA for destruction and it is chopped up. No protein can be made from that mRNA and its corresponding gene.

siRNAs used to treat disease work like natural ones. But they have their own superpowers, Khvorova says. “They’re fully chemically modified.” The tweaks make them stable in the body and send them to the correct organ.
So far, all FDA-approved siRNAs work in the liver. Khvorova’s team is crafting others that can be sent to muscles, nerves or other organs.

Usually, siRNAs don’t completely shut off a gene. But they can meddle enough that very little of its protein gets built, says Judy Lieberman. She’s an immunologist at Boston Children’s Hospital and Harvard Medical School. She was an advisor to the company that first pioneered using siRNAs to treat diseases.

Slowing protein production to just a trickle might help Spider-Man control the level of his superpowers, Lieberman says. He would want enough protein made to make him super, but not enough to cause problems.
Unfortunately, no one has been able to tune siRNAs so precisely.

Spider-Man would also need the inhibitor to work everywhere in his body. That’s not something siRNAs are usually designed to do, says Gane Ka-Shu Wong. He’s a biomedical scientist at the University of Alberta in Edmonton, Canada.
Submit your question here, and we might answer it an upcoming issue of Science News Explores
And there’s one more issue with siRNAs that could be a problem for the web-slinger. “They tend to last,” Wong says. Current siRNA therapies may last for six months or longer with a single dose.

Parker would likely want an inhibitor that breaks down, Wong says. “It’s got to last long enough to get to where it needs to go and shut off whatever it needs to shut off. But it also needs to degrade so that the moment you stop injecting this drug,” the powers return.

Even then, taking the inhibitor off wouldn’t instantly return a superhero’s powers. At a minimum, it could take a few hours to make mRNA copies and get new proteins. But it would probably take longer to return to full power.
“He could reverse it,” Lieberman says, “but it might take a few days.”

title: Experiment: Discover the science behind afterimages
content: *a_brightly_colored_negative_image_of_a_face_against_a_purple_gradient_background,_designed_to_produc

Look at the white dot in the center of the face in the black frame for 30-60 seconds. Then look at a plain white surface. You will see an image that is the same shape and size as the object, but in different colors. This is called an afterimage.
Objective: Investigate color perception by observing afterimages, which are the images left on your retina after you stare at an object and then look away.
Areas of Science: Human Biology & Health
Difficulty: Intermediate medium
Time required: Short (2-5 days)
Prerequisites: A computer with internet access is recommended.
Material availability: Readily available
Cost: Very Low (under $20)
Safety: No issues
Credits: David Whyte, PhD, Science Buddies

We perceive color in the world around us with special sensory cells, called cone cells. Cone cells function in bright light and are responsible for color vision and high-acuity vision, which allows you to see fine details. Cone cells reside in the region at the back of the eye called the fovea. The fovea is quite small, about 1 square millimeter (mm) (0.00155 square inch). It is amazing to think that color and detail we see depends on such a small bit of tissue!

There are three types of cone cells, loosely called blue, green and red, depending on which type of light they respond to best. When you look at a red object, for example, the red cone cells are stimulated. The stimulation of the red cone cells causes them to send a message to the brain, basically saying, “the color of the object is red.”
When blue light and red light are added, it creates the color purple. So when you see the color purple, your blue and your red cone cells are both stimulated.

What about white? If you have seen a rainbow, or the colors produced when sunlight passes through a prism, you have seen for yourself that white light can be separated into different colors. Adding blue, green and red light together produces white light. If you take three flashlights and put red, blue and green filters on them, and shine them all on the same spot, the combined colors produce white light.

Any two colors whose light together produces white are called complementary colors. Examples are red and cyan, green and magenta, blue and yellow. Note that one color in the combination is a primary color, while the other is a mix of the other two primary colors.

When you look at a white image, all three types of cones are stimulated. In other words, the brain interprets the combined input from all three types of cones and tells you that “the color is white.” Note that the way colors of light combine is called additive color mixing, where the three primary colors combine to make white. This is different from the subtractive color mixing you may have learned about when mixing paints together in art class, where if you mix the primary colors together, you will get black.
iFhttps://www.sciencenews.org/conversion/zephr-iframe-test

Looking at a particular color for very long can cause cone cell fatigue — the cone cells get tired. For example, if you stare at a red object, the red cone cells become fatigued and are temporarily unable to respond. If you look at a white area after staring at a red image, you will see an image that is the same size and shape as the original image, but a different color. The image you see on the white surface is called an afterimage. You can see an afterimage by looking at the red circle in Figure 1 in the Experimental Procedure for 30 seconds, then looking at the white region in the square to the right. Can you see the blue-green afterimage?

Why is the afterimage blue-green? When you look at the white surface after staring at the red-colored object, your eyes will essentially receive equal doses of red, green and blue light coming into your eyes, but only the blue and the green cones are able to respond and tell your brain what you are seeing. Because of cone cell fatigue, the input from the red cones is missing from the region of the afterimage. So you see the afterimage as blue-green. (Here is a gross fact! Surgeons wear blue-green scrubs to minimize the afterimage of blood!)

The afterimage disappears after several seconds because the red cone cells recover from their fatigue and become active again. When the red cone cells are active again, all three types of cone cells respond to the white surface, and you see the white region normally. You can even predict the color of the afterimage for most colors — it is the complementary color to the color of the object.
In this human biology project, you will investigate how your cone cells respond to various colors by observing afterimages.

This site, from the University of Washington, has a wealth of information about neuroscience, the eye and afterimages:
A visual illusion based on cone cell fatigue won a contest by the Neural Correlate Society for “The Best Visual Illusion of 2008.” You can see the illusion here:
There are three parts. Each part should take less than one hour.

In Part 1, you will stare at a colored object for various amounts of time, then measure how long it takes for the afterimage to disappear each time. You will then graph the data as Cone stimulation (how long you stared at the colored object) vs. Afterimage persistence (how long before the afterimage disappears). Things to think about: Is there a minimum cone-stimulation time required to produce an afterimage? Do longer cone-stimulation times always cause longer afterimage times, or does the effect level out past a certain time?
In Part 2, you will test whether or not afterimages made by three different colors disappear at the same rate (this measures cone cell recovery).
In Part 3, you will test which color produces an afterimage in the least amount of time (this measures the rate of cone cell fatigue).
